claim: DfE's Generative AI product safety standards, updated 19 January 2026, contain 13 standards, including cognitive development (no final answers, full solutions or complete worked examples by default; track offloading), emotional and social development (function-based language, no human persona) and manipulation (no unjustified confidence).
source: Department for Education (2026). Generative AI: product safety standards. GOV.UK, updated 19 January 2026.
population: England, products used by learners
recommendation: Pitch: eduX already tracks a self-chosen offloading proxy (the just-show-me choice) and teaches hint-first for course questions. It does not detect pasted or copied answers; say so if asked. - State why factual research questions get a full answer plus a checking task (05e). Don't lean on the withdrawn Khanmigo claim. - Check that `text/` describes the chatbot in function-based terms.

Emotional and social development: function-based phrasing, no names or avatars implying personhood. Manipulation: avoid 'absolute, or unjustified confidence'.

population: adults, workplace; not 16–18, not UK

mark_note: arXiv abstract and HTML full text (Table 4): single author Daniele Veri'; 24 focal empirical publications; three direct subjective-objective correlations, REML r = .055, Hartung-Knapp 95% CI [-.047, .156], combined N = 2,765; workplace adults. Unrefereed preprint, and all three correlations come from one research programme.

claim: In Newton's Playground, gold-trophy counts per agent correlated r = .22–.40 with a physics pretest (silver .03–.29), the physics test had Cronbach's alpha .72/.73, and pre-post gain was t(154) = 2.12, p < .05.
source: Shute, V. J., Ventura, M., & Kim, Y. J. (2013). Assessment and learning of qualitative physics in Newton's Playground. Journal of Educational Research, 106(6), 423-430.
effect: gold-trophy r with pretest: ramp .27, lever .22, pendulum .31, springboard .40 (N = 166); pre–post gain t(154) = 2.12, p < .05; pretest–posttest r = .60
population: 167 US 8th–9th graders (about 13–15), one university lab school, about 4 h of play over 1.5 weeks. Not UK, younger than 16–18
recommendation: Use as the benchmark: single in-game indicators correlate about .2–.4 with an external test. Present eduX's target in the same range.
risk: credibility, if we imply our scores are already validated. They're not.
mark_note: Full text: 167 grade 8-9 students at Florida State University School, about 4 h; Table 3 (N = 166) gold .27/.22/.31/.40 and silver .16/.03/.06/.29; Forms A and B are 12 items each, alpha .72/.73; t(154) = 2.12, p < .05; pre-post r = .60. All match.

claim: A stealth assessment of problem solving in Use Your Brainz correlated r = .40 with Raven's Progressive Matrices and r = .41 with MicroDYN (n = 47), with Cronbach's alpha .76 across its four facets.
source: Shute, V. J., Wang, L., Greiff, S., Zhao, W., & Moore, G. (2016). Measuring problem solving skills via stealth assessment in an engaging video game. Computers in Human Behavior, 63, 106-117.
population: 55 US 7th graders (47 analysed), one suburban Illinois school, about 3 h of play. Not UK, younger
recommendation: Cite as the model study design: hours of naturalistic evidence, then two external tests. Our pilot copies this shape.
risk: small n, so wide CI (about .13–.62)
mark_note: Full text: 55 7th graders at a middle school in suburban Illinois, about 3 h on iPad; with n = 47, r = 0.40 (Raven's) and r = 0.41 (MicroDYN), both p < .01; alpha 0.76 across the four facets. All match.

Verifier: 890 results confirmed, but they are configurations x 10 ASAP-SAS items, not results pooled across studies. The 0.37 decoder-encoder gap is on the Fisher-z scale, not raw QWK; the paper says so, and the frequentist estimate is -0.14 and not significant. claim: With single-item reliability of about .17 (back-solved from GLAT alpha .80 with 20 items and a physics test alpha .72 with 12 items), Spearman-Brown implies about 12 observed moments for reliability .70 and 20 for .80, rising to 18 and 30 if per-moment reliability is .12.
source: First-principles calculation: Spearman (1910) and Brown (1910), British Journal of Psychology 3; inputs from Jin et al. (2024) and Shute, Ventura & Kim (2013).
population: n/a
recommendation: Report `n_moments` and "provisional" in progress until about 8 moments (our choice). In the pitch, say how long that takes at a realistic research-question rate.
before_thursday: pitch yes; build once 05e is merged (it is built on branch build/05e-literacy-coaching, not merged to main)
risk: assumes parallel, independent moments. Ask moments come from the same student's similar questions, so reliability may be higher (consistency) or the score narrower (construct under-representation)
mark_note: before_thursday reworded per coordinator: 05e is built on its branch, not merged. Verifier: Recomputed. Back-solved rho1 = .80/(20-19*.80) = .167; .72 with 12 items (NP Form A, confirmed 12 items) gives .176. Spearman-Brown k = R(1-r)/(r(1-R)): at .17, 11.4 -> 12 and 19.5 -> 20; at .12, 17.1 -> 18 and 29.3 -> 30.

claim: eduX's AI-literacy parts use the course decay (base half-life 2 days, doubled on success), so a part at 0.75 after one correct moment falls to about 0.22 a week later.

claim: On a four-option opportunity-cost item, only 21.6% of 199 economists and PhD students at the 2005 ASSA meetings chose the intended answer ($10), while the wrong options $0, $40 and $50 drew 25.1%, 25.6% and 27.6%.
source: Ferraro, P.J. & Taylor, L.O. (2005). Do economists recognize an opportunity cost when they see one? A dismal performance from the dismal science. Contributions to Economic Analysis & Policy 4(1), Article 7.

recommendation: Use the structure (one key and three single-error distractors) as the demo opportunity-cost check, written in our own UK wording. Add rows 1–3.

claim: Among 358 US students in the first week of introductory microeconomics, those who had taken a previous economics course answered the opportunity-cost item correctly less often (7.4%) than those who had not (17.2%), a significant difference (chi-squared 7.13, p = 0.008).

mark_note: Full text: 358 undergraduates in week 1 of Intro Micro; 270 (76%) with a prior macro or high-school course, 86 (24%) without; 7.4% vs 17.2% correct; Pearson chi2 = 7.13, p = 0.008.

claim: In 431 first-year students, the opportunity-cost subscore on the Test of Economic Literacy barely changed over a semester (mean 3.58 to 3.68 out of 5), acquisition depended more on background than on teaching, and it was only weakly related to final course performance.
source: Shanahan, M.P., Foster, G. & Meyer, J.H.F. (2006). Operationalising a threshold concept in economics: a pilot study using multiple choice questions on opportunity cost. International Review of Economics Education 5(2), 29-57.

risk: credibility (pilot measure with acknowledged measurement error)
mark_note: Full text: UniSA introductory economics, n = 431; first TEL OC 3.58 (1.29), last 3.68 (1.23), difference 0.10 (1.42), scale 0-5. The conclusion states acquisition depends more on background than the classroom and is weakly related to final performance. r = .45 is OC exam level vs final percent; the OC change vs final percent is r = .01.

claim: Davies and Mangan classify marginality, opportunity cost, incentives and cumulative causation as discipline threshold concepts in economics, and comparative statics (equilibrium, ceteris paribus), time and elasticity as modelling concepts, and recommend assessing them with unfamiliar problems that do not name the model.

claim: In the TUCE-4 matched norming sample, 43% before and 32% after a principles course chose business demand as the limit of productive capacity, 36% before and 28% after chose falling long-run economic profits when competitive firms' costs rise, and 33% before and 29% after chose that firms would pay a pollution tax rather than cut production; overall percent correct rose from about 31-33% to 43-47%.

claim: At the start of term, 69% (control) and 77% (treatment) of first-year economics students agreed that rent controls make housing available to more families; information reduced but did not eliminate this belief. source: Brandts, J., Busom, I., Lopez-Mayan, C. & Panadés, J. (2022). Dispelling misconceptions about economics. Journal of Economic Psychology 88, 102461 (doi:10.1016/j.joep.2021.102461); figures from the BSE Focus summary 'Dispelling Misconceptions about Rent Control'.

recommendation: Add row 12. Because a single correction partly fades, keep the misconception in reviews: correct evidence clears it, but a review re-tests it.

Verifier: Checked against the authors' BSE Focus summary only: 69% control and 77% treatment at the start (UAB, 340/272); lab 84/75/83% (Valencia, n = 172); disagreement rose 16-22%; the belief was not eliminated. claim: In Mayer's summary table of multimedia-learning experiments, coherence had a median effect size of 0.86 (18 of 19 tests positive), signaling 0.70 (26 of 28), segmenting 0.67 (7 of 7), pre-training 0.78 (10 of 10), modality 1.00 (18 of 19) and redundancy 0.10 (8 of 12).
source: Mayer, R. E. Research-based principles for designing multimedia instruction. Chapter in Society for the Teaching of Psychology e-book Applying the Science of Learning in Education (updated edition; tables based on Mayer, 2021, Multimedia Learning, 3rd ed., Cambridge University Press)
evidence_strength: theory (a narrative summary of the author's own experiments, with median effect sizes; not a systematic meta-analysis)
effect: median d: coherence 0.86, signalling 0.70, segmenting 0.67, pre-training 0.78, modality 1.00, redundancy 0.10; no CIs reported
population: mostly university students in lab experiments, US. Not 16–18 and not UK.
recommendation: Build the video as seven labelled segments, with one keyword and one highlight box per shot, no music or stock footage, a pre-training diagram before the demo, and narration as the main channel (captions as a separate track). Applying this to persuading judges is our analogy.
risk: credibility, if presented as evidence that the *pitch* works. These are lab learning effects, and the author's own summary may be optimistic compared with independent meta-analyses (see 02 and 03).
mark_note: Full text Tables 2 and 3 (based on Mayer 2021): coherence 18 of 19, 0.86; signaling 26 of 28, 0.70; redundancy 8 of 12, 0.10; segmenting 7 of 7, 0.67; pre-training 10 of 10, 0.78; modality 18 of 19, 1.00. Population 'mostly US university students' is not stated in the chapter.

claim: A meta-analysis of 44 independent effect sizes from 29 experimental studies with 2,726 participants found signaling associated with increased learning outcomes, d = 0.38.

effect: d = 0.38 (p < .01); CI not in the abstract
population: mixed grade levels (coded as a moderator); not UK-specific
recommendation: Keep the highlight boxes on the plan's first line and on the `state` row that changes. Use one cue at a time.
risk: low. Over-signalling (many cues) is a known boundary condition.
mark_note: Abstract-level only (publisher page paywalled; abstract text seen via search snippets): 44 effect sizes, 29 studies, 2,726 participants, d = .38, p < .01. ETR&D 68(5):2095-2119. Not retracted (OpenAlex).

claim: A signaling meta-analysis (reported as 103 studies, 12,201 participants) found cues improved retention g = 0.53 and transfer g = 0.33 (figures from secondary reports).

population: mostly university students; not UK
recommendation: Signalling helps people remember *what* was shown more than reason with it. Use it for the one fact judges must retain ("server never calls an AI model"; "the letter is scored by the server").
risk: the numbers are unverified against the primary source; cite as secondary.
mark_note: Secondary source only (TUM Clearing House Unterricht summary): 103 studies, 12,201 participants (~14% secondary pupils), retention g = 0.53, transfer g = 0.33 (70 comparisons). CIs and k=139 not checked. Published 2018 (online 2017), ERR 23:1-24.

effect: "small to medium" (no numbers in the abstract)
population: mostly university students; not UK
recommendation: Seven named segments, with a keyword change at each cut (§A). In the live demo, pause after each reply and say what changed before the next message. Already cited in step 05d for teaching; here it is reused for the video.

claim: A meta-analysis found that including seductive details (interesting but irrelevant information) in learning materials can hinder learning, with effects moderated by factors including learner pacing and delivery format.

population: mixed; not UK-specific
recommendation: No stock footage of classrooms, no music under narration, and no team-backstory shots in the 2:30. Put the team on the end card only.
risk: low. Builds on 1-14; not new evidence.
mark_note: Secondary only (publisher abstract not readable). ACU Inspire summary: 68 effects from 58 studies, g = -0.33; larger negative effect when learners cannot control pace, and for static details, text+image, and paper vs digital. Consistent with claim. EPR 32(3):707-734.

claim: In eight hospitals in eight cities, introducing a 19-item surgical safety checklist was associated with deaths falling from 1.5% to 0.8% and inpatient complications from 11.0% to 7.0%, comparing 3,733 patients before with 3,955 after.

risk: low. Don't cite it in the pitch; it's a team-process tool.
mark_note: Abstract only (cap): 19-item checklist, 8 hospitals in 8 cities (8 countries), 3,733 before / 3,955 after, patients 16+, noncardiac surgery; deaths 1.5% -> 0.8% (P=0.003); complications 11.0% -> 7.0% (P<0.001). All numbers match. NEJM 360(5):491-499.

claim: Degani and Wiener's NASA contractor report analyses the functions, format, design, length and use of the normal flight-deck checklist against human limitations and ends with design guidelines.

Verifier: Tunguz page confirms pitches 'oscillate between what is and what could be' but does not mention ending with the reward ('new bliss'). risk: older model. Newer reasoning models may self-check better, though w2-02-40 suggests that holds only where verification is cheap.

claim: Across five LLMs including GPT-4, verbalised confidence tended to be overconfident and calibration and failure prediction improved with model capability, while white-box methods did better than black-box ones only narrowly (abstract example: AUROC 0.522 to 0.605).
source: Xiong, M. et al. (2024). Can LLMs express their uncertainty? An empirical evaluation of confidence elicitation in LLMs. ICLR 2024. arXiv:2306.13063.
effect: AUROC 0.522 vs 0.605, black-box vs white-box (abstract example)
population: Five dataset types (incl. commonsense and arithmetic reasoning); five LLMs incl. GPT-4 and LLaMA 2 Chat
recommendation: Keep the confidence part ("tone isn't a check"). Don't ask the chatbot for a confidence label. Kadavath et al. (2022, arXiv:2207.05221) found good calibration only from token probabilities in the right format, which eduX can't see.
risk: the AUROC pair is one example in the abstract, not an average across models.
mark_note: Claim rewritten: abstract does not say which value is black-box and which white-box. Verifier: Abstract only: overconfident verbalised confidence; calibration and failure prediction improve with capability; white-box better but gap narrow, 'e.g., 0.522 to 0.605 in AUROC'. The abstract does not say which value is black-box and which white-box; the claim's mapping is an inference.

claim: In April 2025 automated tests, models falsely claimed to have used a code tool in o3 5.0% (zero-shot) / 12.8% (few-shot), o1 13.0% / 30.1%, o3-mini 8.3% / 18.0%, GPT-4.1 1.8% / 7.0% and GPT-4o 0.8% / 3.0% of conversations.
source: Transluce (2025, 16 April). Investigating truthfulness in a pre-release o3 model.
evidence_strength: practitioner (red-team audit). The analogy to eduX is speculative.
population: Adversarial automated conversations: 400 zero-shot, 500 few-shot (2,000 for o3)
recommendation: Prefer a school deployment setting for "search on/off" over the chatbot's self-report. Include a "claims it searched" case in the audit (rec 3, 6).
risk: narrow, adversarial prompts. The authors warn against generalising.
mark_note: Transluce, 16 Apr 2025: o3 5.0/12.8, o1 13.0/30.1, o3-mini 8.3/18.0, GPT-4.1 1.8/7.0, GPT-4o 0.8/3.0; 400 zero-shot, 500 few-shot (2,000 for o3); 71 o3 laptop claims. Authors warn this is a narrow slice of prompt space.

claim: A meta-analysis of 28 studies found 25.4% (95% CI 19.5-32.4) of quotations in medical journal articles were inaccurate and 11.9% (95% CI 8.4-16.6) were major errors.
source: Jergas, H. & Baethge, C. (2015). Quotation accuracy in medical journal articles: a systematic review and meta-analysis. PeerJ 3, e1364.
field: research integrity (cross-field analogy: human citation practice)
effect: pooled proportions with CIs as above
population: Published medical journal articles (28 studies)
recommendation: Pitch: "check the source says it" is a general literacy skill, and chatbots with search fail in the same way humans do (rec 7).
risk: don't imply chatbots are "as good as humans". The rates aren't measured on the same tasks.
mark_note: 28 studies; total errors 25.4% (95% CI 19.5-32.4); major errors 11.9% (8.4-16.6). The results text gives the upper bound as 32.5, a minor inconsistency in the paper.

claim: Wardle's First Draft typology sorts information disorder into seven types (satire or parody, false connection, misleading content, false context, imposter content, manipulated content, fabricated content), and Snopes uses ratings including Misattributed, Miscaptioned and Outdated alongside True/False.
source: Wardle, C. (2017). Fake news. It's complicated. First Draft (seven types as reproduced at https://library.queens.edu/misinformation-on-social-media/definitions); Snopes, Fact check ratings, https://www.snopes.com/ratings/ (definitions via secondary copy https://propagandacritic.com/?p=112).
population: Public misinformation (journalism practice)
recommendation: Map eduX parts to fact-checker categories: - fabricated → fabrication - misattributed / false connection → misattribution - outdated → cutoff - false context → later Use the same words in the student-facing feedback, so the skill carries over to news.
risk: Wardle's categories include intent to deceive, and chatbots have none. Keep "no intent" in the fabrication point.
mark_note: The seven Wardle types are confirmed only via a secondary (Queens library) page; the First Draft original was not checked. snopes.com/ratings returned HTTP 402, so the Snopes rating names are unverified first-hand (secondary copy only).

claim: A meta-analysis of 57 experiments (336 tests) found case-comparison activities produced greater learning than sequential, single-case or non-analogous cases and traditional instruction (d = .50, 95% CI [.44, .56]), with larger effects when learners searched for similarities, the principle was given after comparison, content was perceptual, and testing was immediate.
source: Alfieri, L., Nokes-Malach, T. J., & Schunn, C. D. (2013). Learning through case comparisons: A meta-analytic review. Educational Psychologist, 48(2), 87-113.
population: Mixed laboratory and classroom studies; ages not stated in abstract; not UK-specific
recommendation: rec 1. Contrast the twin concept in `reteach` when a declared confusable pair is involved: similarity prompt first, principle after. Pairs come from w1-04 (contestability/competition, price discrimination/product differentiation, XED/YED/PED signs, current account/budget deficit).
effort: S (reuses the existing `confusable` edges and block)
risk: credibility. The effect is stronger for perceptual content and immediate tests, while economics concepts are verbal and the exam is delayed, so expect less than d = .50. Contrasting a wrong idea with a right one could also seed the wrong one; show both as correct concepts, not as a right/wrong pair.
mark_note: Abstract only (OpenAlex): 57 experiments, 336 tests, d = .50 [.44, .56], 4 of 15 moderators (similarities objective, principle after comparison, perceptual content, immediate test) all match. Capped at ~ because full text not read. No retraction found.

claim: In 3rd-12th grade classrooms, students who self-graded performed better on subsequent tests (g = .34) and peer-graders also benefited (g = .29); student grades did not differ much from teacher grades (g = .04) and correlated r = .67 (self) with them.
source: Sanchez, C. E., Atkinson, K. M., Koenka, A. C., Moshontz, H., & Cooper, H. (2017). Self-grading and peer-grading for formative and summative assessments in 3rd through 12th grade classrooms: A meta-analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(8), 1049-1066.
effect: self-grading g = .34 (CI not in abstract); peer-grading g = .29; self vs teacher grade difference g = .04; r = .67 with teacher grades
population: Grades 3-12 classrooms; country not stated in abstract
recommendation: rec 2. Before feedback on an explain-back or past question, the student self-marks against the part's point titles. Feedback names agreement and mismatch. The self-mark never enters `p_known`.
risk: the authors flag few studies for the moderators. Students who struggle with writing may under-claim, so feedback must be specific, never "you overrated yourself". No self-mark data is shown to teachers (same rule as confidence, §2.4).
mark_note: Abstract only: g = .34 self, .29 peer, g = .04 vs teacher for both, r = .67 self / .68 peer, grades 3-12 all match. Abstract also notes the self-grading benefit was larger in randomised studies and the evidence base is small. Full text not read.

claim: A meta-analysis of 14 studies (16 comparisons, N = 1,213) found drawing support that facilitated integration raised comprehension (g = 0.35), whereas support not expected to facilitate integration did not (g = -0.15), and drawing support in general was not related to outcomes.
source: Leutner, D., & Biele, J. (2025). Without integration, everything is nothing: A meta-analysis of the effectiveness of instructional support for drawing-to-learn. Educational Psychology Review, 37(4).
effect: integration support g = 0.35; non-integration support g = −0.15 (n.s.); CIs not in abstract
population: Mostly science learners; ages not stated in abstract; not UK-specific
recommendation: rec 4. For `diagram` parts: sketch on paper, then state which curve shifts, which direction, and the effect on P and Q, then compare with the reference description. Never a bare "draw it".
risk: the chatbot can't see the sketch. The scored evidence is the verbal integration answer, not the drawing, so don't claim to assess diagrams.
mark_note: Abstract only (OpenAlex + publisher snippet): 14 studies, 16 comparisons, N = 1,213; integration-facilitating support g = 0.35 (significant), other support g = -0.15 (n.s.); general support unrelated to outcomes. All match. Issue listed as 37(4) on OpenAlex but 37(1), art. 93 in one citation; minor. Full text paywall-redirected.

claim: In an introductory psychology class with three practice sessions two days apart after each lecture, where correct fill-in-the-blank items were dropped and incorrect items repeated up to two more times per session, successive relearning produced better end-of-semester recall than restudying with exposure duration controlled.
source: Higham, P. A., Zengel, B., Bartlett, L. K., & Hadwin, J. A. (2022). The benefits of successive relearning on multiple learning outcomes. Journal of Educational Psychology, 114(5), 928-944.
effect: not reported in the abstract (direction only)
population: University introductory psychology students (authors at University of Southampton, UK; country not stated in abstract); not 16-18
outcome: learning (recall). Also self-reported mastery, attentional control and anxiety (correlational within the relearning group)
recommendation: rec 3. Re-ask a missed review once more later in the same session, up to 2 times. A within-session re-ask is not a new spaced review and gets no half-life growth.
risk: more items per session for weak students, so fatigue and stop rules must win. The cue was fill-in-the-blank, not MCQ.
mark_note: Abstract only: intro psych course, 3 sessions 2 days apart, 20 fill-in-blank items, correct dropped, incorrect repeated up to 2 more times, 10 weeks, exposure controlled, better end-of-semester recall than restudy. All match. Country not in abstract. 114(5), 928-944 correct.

claim: A meta-analysis of 53 studies (166 comparisons) found problem solving before instruction outperformed instruction first (g = 0.36, 95% CI [0.20, 0.51]), more so with high fidelity to Productive Failure (g 0.37-0.58), with instruction-first favoured for 2nd-5th graders on domain-general skills, and a publication-bias-adjusted estimate of g = 0.87.
source: Sinha, T., & Kapur, M. (2021). When problem solving followed by instruction works: Evidence for productive failure. Review of Educational Research, 91(5), 761-798.
population: Mixed school and university learners; not UK-specific
recommendation: no change. Keep the single pre-question. The gain depends on a designed consolidation phase that chat can't guarantee (confirms 2-06).
risk: credibility, if the 0.87 bias-adjusted figure is quoted without the caveats.
mark_note: Claim rewritten: 'and' corrected to 'on' (one combined condition). Verifier: Abstract only: 53 studies, 166 comparisons, g = 0.36 [0.20, 0.51], high-fidelity PF g 0.37-0.58, bias-adjusted g = 0.87 all match. Abstract says I-PS favoured for 2nd-5th graders on domain-general skills (a combined condition), so 'and' in the claim should read 'on'.

claim: A meta-analysis of 86 studies and 445 effect sizes found a generation effect on memory of about d = 0.40.
source: Bertsch, S., Pesta, B. J., Wiscott, R., & McDaniel, M. A. (2007). The generation effect: A meta-analytic review. Memory & Cognition, 35(2), 201-210. Abstract: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17645161/
effect: d ≈ 0.40 (CI not given in our source)
population: Mostly adult laboratory participants; not 16-18; not UK
recommendation: no new feature. It supports keeping the hint level's "last step left for them" and the pre-questions. Cite it in research.md as backing for those.
risk: low. Don't extend generation to novices at `worked_example` (expertise reversal, CSV 2-01).
mark_note: Abstract only (Europe PMC): 86 studies, 445 effect sizes, mean generation effect .40. Matches. Full text not read.

claim: Across 642 independent tests, implementation intentions improved cognitive, affective and behavioural outcomes (.27 <= d <= .66), with larger effects for if-then format, high goal motivation and rehearsed plans.
source: Sheeran, P., Listrom, O., & Gollwitzer, P. M. (2024). The when and how of planning: Meta-analysis of the scope and components of implementation intentions in 642 tests. European Review of Social Psychology, 36(1), 162-194.
effect: .27 ≤ d ≤ .66 across outcome types (uncorrected). A bias-corrected estimate is reported by secondary sources only; not claimed
population: Mixed, mostly adults; not 16-18-specific; not UK-specific
outcome: mixed (behaviour, cognition, affect), mostly not grades
recommendation: rec 7. An optional, student-written, exam-directed if-then plan at most once a week, kept in the chat. No reminders.
risk: manipulation risk if it turns into "commit to coming back" (DfE). Publication bias means the true effect is smaller.
mark_note: Abstract only: 642 independent tests, .27 <= d <= .66 across cognitive, affective and behavioural outcomes; larger effects with if-then format, high motivation and rehearsal. Matches. Published online 2024; volume 36(1) is dated 2025.

claim: Mental contrasting with implementation intentions led 66 second-year high-school students to complete over 60% more practice questions for a high-stakes exam, and improved 77 low-income urban US 5th graders' report-card grades (partial eta-squared = .07), attendance (.05) and conduct (.07) against a positive-thinking control.
source: Duckworth, A. L., Grant, H., Loew, B., Oettingen, G., & Gollwitzer, P. M. (2011). Self-regulation strategies improve self-discipline in adolescents. Educational Psychology, 31(1), 17-26; Duckworth, A. L., Kirby, T. A., Gollwitzer, A., & Oettingen, G. (2013). From fantasy to action: MCII improves academic performance in children. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 4(6), 745-753.
effect: practice questions +60% (no SD-based effect size in the abstract); grades η² = .07
population: High-school 2nd-year students (n = 66; country not stated in abstract); US urban 5th graders (n = 77)
recommendation: don't build beyond rec 7. Usable in the pitch only as "planning raised practice", not as a learning gain.
risk: overclaiming. The 2011 outcome is practice volume, not scores.
mark_note: Claim rewritten: values are partial eta-squared; country of the 2011 study not stated. Verifier: Abstracts only. 2011: 66 second-year high-school students, >60% more practice questions; matches, but the abstract does not name the country (authors are US/German). 2013: 77 low-income urban 5th graders, partial eta2 = .07 grades, .05 attendance, .07 conduct vs a positive-thinking control; matches (these are partial eta-squared values).

claim: Randomly assigning more than 9,000 students at three colleges to one of two separate programmes (an online planning module, or text reminders or coaching) produced precise null effects on credit accumulation, course grades and retention.
source: Oreopoulos, P., Patterson, R. W., Petronijevic, U., & Pope, N. G. (2022). Low-touch attempts to improve time management among traditional and online college students. Journal of Human Resources, 57(1), 1-43.
effect: precise nulls (point estimates not in the abstract)
population: College students at three North American institutions; not 16-18; not UK
recommendation: don't build planning or reminder features expecting grade gains. Cite in the pitch Q&A as the reason eduX puts its effort into teaching moves, not nudges.
risk: none for eduX. It is a guard against overclaiming.
mark_note: Claim rewritten: two separate programmes, not one module with texts; study time rose marginally. Verifier: Abstract only: >9,000 students, 3 colleges, precise nulls on credits, grades and retention; matches. The abstract describes two separate programmes (an online planning module, and text reminders or coaching), not one module 'with' texts; slight conflation. Study time rose marginally.

claim: A soft (non-binding) commitment device raised exam sign-up, participation and passing among German university students while a pure reminder did not, and in a Stanford MOOC a commitment device raised course completion by 40%, performance by 0.29 SD and time on course by 24%, while alert and distraction-blocking tools had no significant effect.
source: Himmler, O., Jäckle, R., & Weinschenk, P. (2019). Soft commitments, reminders, and academic performance. American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, 11(2), 114-142; Patterson, R. W. (2018). Can behavioral tools improve online student outcomes? Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, 153, 293-321.
effect: Himmler: not in abstract (direction only). Patterson: +0.29 SD performance, +40% completion, +24% time on course
population: German university business administration first-years; adult MOOC learners (n = 657 per secondary sources); not 16-18; not UK
outcome: progression (exam participation and passing); learning (course performance) and engagement (time) for Patterson
recommendation: don't build commitment contracts. eduX has no deadlines it owns, and return commitments are engagement-prolonging. If ever, let the school's own exam timetable be the anchor; it already is, via exam-anchored spacing.
risk: manipulation (DfE standards); pressure on minors.
mark_note: Abstracts only. Himmler: soft commitment raised exam sign-up, participation and passing; pure reminder had no effect. Matches, but the abstract does not state the German university or business-administration population. Patterson: commitment device +40% completion, +0.29 SD grades, +24% time; alert and blocking tools no different from control. Matches. n = 657 not verified.

claim: The EEF's independent trial of texting GCSE-resit students and/or their study supporters in English FE colleges found no effect on English or maths resit pass rates (0 months' progress in each arm, high security), whereas the earlier EEF Texting Parents trial in 36 secondary schools (about 16,000 pupils) reported about one month's additional progress in maths.
source: Education Endowment Foundation, Texting Students and Study Supporters (project page and evaluation report); Miller, S., Davison, J., Yohanis, J., Sloan, S., Gildea, A., & Thurston, A. (2016). Texting Parents: Evaluation report and executive summary. EEF. (Figures from search snippets of EEF pages; pages returned 403.)
effect: TSSS: 0 months' progress, all arms. Texting Parents: about +1 month, maths (effect size not retrieved)
population: UK FE college students aged 16-19 resitting GCSE English/maths; UK secondary pupils (Texting Parents)
recommendation: don't add messaging. Use as pitch Q&A evidence that nudges alone don't move 16–19 resit results in the UK.
risk: credibility. Verify the EEF figures against the report before quoting them on a slide.
mark_note: Secondary sources only; the EEF pages return 403. A search summary of the EEF page gives 0 months' progress in both arms (supporters-only, and students+supporters) on GCSE resit pass rates, high security, 3,779 students in 31 English FE colleges. Not confirmed per subject or from the report itself. Texting Parents: Schools Week (15 Jul 2016) confirms 36 schools, nearly 16,000 secondary pupils, +1 month maths.

claim: In two large online experiments with a maths game (about 10,000 and 70,000 subjects), easier versions almost always produced more engagement and longer play, and the most engaging conditions produced the slowest learning.
source: Lomas, D., Patel, K., Forlizzi, J., & Koedinger, K. R. (2013). Optimizing challenge in an educational game using large-scale design experiments. Proceedings of CHI 2013, 89-98.
population: Anonymous online game players; age not verified; not UK
recommendation: rec 8. Pitch line: eduX sets difficulty for learning (`p_now`), not time-on-app. No retention-driven easing.
risk: low. Don't overgeneralise from a number-line game.
mark_note: Abstract only: about 10,000 and 70,000 subjects; easier versions almost always gave more engagement and longer play; the most engaging conditions had the slowest learning. Matches. Design dimensions not checked.

claim: Maximum-information item selection in computerised adaptive testing (1PL or 2PL) results in each test-taker answering about 50% of items correctly, and selecting items for maximum information at a shifted ability level gives satisfactory easier or harder tests under both models while probability-point selection works only under 1PL.
source: Eggen, T. J. H. M., & Verschoor, A. J. (2006). Optimal testing with easy or difficult items in computerized adaptive testing. Applied Psychological Measurement, 30(5), 379-393.
effect: about 50% correct under maximum information; precision cost of easier tests not in the abstract
population: Simulated test-takers; no humans
recommendation: - rec 10 (later): once items are calibrated, select reviews at a shifted ability; the target is our choice. - rec 5 (now, speculative transfer of exposure control): rotate which misconceptions appear as distractors when a part has more than three.
risk: the link from test-security exposure control to learning is our analogy, not a tested effect. Rotation must still always include a held misconception.
mark_note: Abstract only: maximum-information selection (1PL or 2PL) gives about 50% correct; probability-point selection works only under 1PL; shifted-ability maximum information is satisfactory under both models. Matches.

claim: A 19-item surgical safety checklist in 8 hospitals was associated with deaths falling from 1.5% to 0.8% and complications from 11.0% to 7.0% (pre/post), but mandated adoption across 101 Ontario hospitals found no significant change in mortality (0.71% to 0.65%; OR 0.91, 95% CI 0.80-1.03) or complications (3.86% to 3.82%; OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.90-1.03).
source: Haynes, A. B., et al. (2009). A surgical safety checklist to reduce morbidity and mortality in a global population. NEJM, 360(5), 491-499; Urbach, D. R., et al. (2014). Introduction of surgical safety checklists in Ontario, Canada. NEJM, 370(11), 1029-1038.
population: Surgical patients aged 16+ in 8 international hospitals; Ontario surgical patients (analogy only)
recommendation: rec 9 (pitch framing). A self-check works when it is specific and owned (the self-mark in rec 2), not when mandated as a ritual. **Speculative analogy.**
risk: credibility, if presented as education evidence. It isn't.
mark_note: Abstracts only (NEJM returned 403). Haynes: 19 items, 8 hospitals, 3,733/3,955 patients aged 16+, deaths 1.5% to 0.8%, complications 11.0% to 7.0%. Urbach: 101 hospitals, 109,341/106,370 procedures, mortality 0.71% to 0.65% OR 0.91 [0.80, 1.03], complications 3.86% to 3.82% OR 0.97 [0.90, 1.03]. All match.

claim: Deliberate practice explained 26% of performance variance in games, 21% in music, 18% in sports, 4% in education and less than 1% in professions.
source: Macnamara, B. N., Hambrick, D. Z., & Oswald, F. L. (2014). Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: A meta-analysis. Psychological Science, 25(8), 1608-1618.
effect: R² by domain as in the claim
population: Mixed domains and ages; not UK-specific
recommendation: rec 9. In the pitch, don't claim "more practice time → mastery". eduX's mechanism is targeted feedback on named gaps, which is the "deliberate" part, not the hours.
risk: low. It is correlational, and definitions of deliberate practice are disputed (Ericsson's replies).
mark_note: Abstract only: games 26%, music 21%, sports 18%, education 4%, professions <1%. Matches.

claim: Forty participants who learned foreign vocabulary to criterion in two sessions 12 hours apart needed half as much relearning practice and retained better at 1 week and 6 months when they slept between sessions than when both sessions were on the same day.
source: Mazza, S., Gerbier, E., Gustin, M.-P., Kasikci, Z., Koenig, O., Toppino, T. C., & Magnin, M. (2016). Relearn faster and retain longer: Along with practice, sleep makes perfect. Psychological Science, 27(10), 1321-1330.
effect: relearning practice halved; retention effect sizes not in the abstract
population: 40 adult participants (abstract); foreign vocabulary; not 16-18; not UK
recommendation: rec 6. One optional line in `offer_stop` ("a quick go tomorrow will stick better than more tonight"). No sleep tracking or profiling.
risk: low. Don't present it as eduX evidence.
mark_note: Abstract only: 40 participants, vocabulary learned to criterion in two sessions 12 h apart (sleep group vs same-day morning/evening group), relearning practice halved, better retention at 1 week and 6 months. Matches. Participant ages not in abstract.

claim: The 9EC0 A level is three 2-hour, 100-mark papers weighted 35%, 35% and 30%; Papers 1 and 2 have Section A (multiple-choice and short-answer), Section B (one data response) and Section C (one extended answer from a choice of two), Paper 3 has two data-response questions each including a choice of extended answer, and AO3 and AO4 are each 26-28% of the qualification while AO1 and AO2 are each 22-24%.
source: Pearson Edexcel Level 3 Advanced GCE in Economics A (9EC0) Specification, Issue 2, October 2016, pp. 2-4 and 39-42.
population: 9EC0 candidates, England
recommendation: pitch line that AO3 (analysis) plus AO4 (evaluation) is 52–56% of the qualification
risk: low. A later issue may exist (not checked); it would be unlikely to change the structure.
mark_note: Spec Issue 2 (Oct 2016) pp.2-4, 41-42 (text extracted from the cited mirror): three 2-hour 100-mark papers, 35/35/30; P1/P2 Sections A (MCQ + short answer), B (one data response), C (choose 1 of 2 extended), 7 questions; P3 two sections each one data-response question incl. choice of extended answer, 2 questions; AO1/AO2 22-24%, AO3/AO4 26-28% (P3 weights AO3/AO4 8-10%). Mirror is third-party; Issue 2 may not be the latest Pearson issue.

claim: In the June 2025 9EC0 mark schemes, Papers 1 and 2 each have about 38 point-marked and 62 level-marked marks out of 100 and Paper 3 has about 26 and 74; multiple choice is 5 marks on each of Papers 1 and 2 and none on Paper 3, giving roughly 34% point-marked, 66% level-marked and 3.5% multiple choice when weighted 35/35/30.
source: Pearson Edexcel, Mark Scheme (Results) Summer 2025, GCE Economics A 9EC0 Papers 01, 02 and 03; cross-checked with Summer 2023 Papers 01 and 03.
population: 9EC0 candidates, England
recommendation: frame MCQs as diagnosis and chain and evaluation checks as the route to marks (rec 1); prioritise step 07
risk: credibility, if the figures are stated more exactly than they are. Section A splits vary by year. Say "about".
mark_note: Checked Summer 2025 MS for P01-P03 (Pearson PDFs). P1/P2: 5 MCQ x1 mark (Section A 25 marks); Q6 parts 5, 8 (K2A2An2E2), 12 (8+4), 10 (6+4), 15 (9+6) [P2 orders 10 then 12]; Q7/8 25 (16+9) -> 38 point / 62 level. P3: per question 5, 8, 12 (8+4), 25 (16+9) -> 26/74. Evaluation marks 25/25/30. Weighted 34.4% point, 3.5% MCQ. 2023 cross-check not verified.

claim: The 8-mark data-response parts in 9EC0 are point-marked as Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2 and Evaluation 2, so 2 evaluation marks in each such question are point-marked rather than levelled.
source: Pearson Edexcel, Mark Scheme (Results) Summer 2025, 9EC0 Papers 01 Q6(b), 02 Q6(b), 03 Q1(b) and Q2(b); Summer 2023 Paper 01 Q6(c), Paper 03 Q1(b) and Q2(b).
population: 9EC0 candidates, England
recommendation: build evaluation practice first on these point-marked marks (rec 4)
risk: low
mark_note: 2025 MS: P1 6(b), P2 6(b), P3 1(b) and 2(b) all 'Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 2' with point marking (1+1). 2023 references not checked.

claim: Solving two-dimensional Parsons problems with distractors took significantly less time than fixing or writing equivalent code, with no statistically significant difference in learning performance or retention one week later.
source: Ericson, B.J., Margulieux, L.E. & Rick, J. (2017). Solving Parsons problems versus fixing and writing code. Proceedings of the 17th Koli Calling International Conference on Computing Education Research, 20-29.
evidence_strength: experimental comparison (assignment method not read; abstract only)
population: introductory programming learners (not stated in abstract)
recommendation: ordering is a cheap warm-up (C2), not the main check
risk: credibility. Equal learning on a code test is not essay transfer.
mark_note: Abstract matches exactly (2D Parsons with distractors significantly less time than fixing/writing; no significant difference in learning performance or one-week retention). Abstract-only.

claim: In CS1 exams, Parsons problem scores showed notable correlation with code-writing scores and low correlation with code tracing.
source: Denny, P., Luxton-Reilly, A. & Simon, B. (2008). Evaluating a new exam question: Parsons problems. Proceedings of ICER 2008, 113-124.
population: university CS1 exam takers
recommendation: chain ordering may be a usable *diagnostic* of analysis skill, not proof of it
risk: correlation ≠ training effect
mark_note: Abstract: notable correlation between Parsons and code-writing scores; low correlation between Parsons and tracing (and between writing and tracing). Abstract-only.

claim: In a CS1 classroom study with 237 consenting students (50 and 43 analysed in the two quantitative studies), Faded Parsons Problems beat code writing and code tracing for learning programming patterns and improved code writing comparably to code-writing practice, while the authors report their earlier plain Parsons problems did not transfer to writing code for the same question.
source: Weinman, N., Fox, A. & Hearst, M.A. (2021). Improving Instruction of Programming Patterns with Faded Parsons Problems. Proceedings of CHI 2021.
population: US university CS1 students
recommendation: prefer the missing-link check (C1) to ordering alone
risk: the analogy (code to economic chain) is speculative
mark_note: Abstract confirms classroom study with 237 students; FPPs significantly surpass code writing and tracing for patterns; improve code writing comparably to code-writing exercises. The 50/43 analysed and the statement about earlier plain Parsons problems not transferring could not be checked (ACM full text 403).

claim: A review of Parsons-problem research concluded that their effectiveness as a question type and as a learning tool remains uncertain due to a lack of replicated research.
source: Du, Y., Luxton-Reilly, A. & Denny, P. (2020). A Review of Research on Parsons Problems. Proceedings of the Australasian Computing Education Conference (ACE 2020).
population: introductory CS students (studies reviewed)
recommendation: call the Parsons evidence "promising, unreplicated" in pitch and Q&A
risk: low
mark_note: Abstract states effectiveness as question type and learning tool remains uncertain due to lack of replicated research. Abstract-only (the claim is the abstract's conclusion).

claim: A meta-analysis of writing interventions for grades 4-12 (123 documents, 154 effect sizes on writing quality) found weighted mean effects of 0.82 for strategy instruction, 0.82 summarisation, 0.75 peer assistance, 0.70 setting product goals, 0.50 sentence combining, 0.32 prewriting, 0.25 study of models and -0.32 grammar instruction.
source: Graham, S. & Perin, D. (2007). A meta-analysis of writing instruction for adolescent students. Journal of Educational Psychology 99(3), 445-476.
population: grades 4-12, mostly US
recommendation: plan-skeleton step (rec 9), per-strand goals (step 07), C4 criteria sorting; no grammar drills
risk: small study counts per category; writing quality is not exam levels
mark_note: Abstract confirms 123 documents, 154 ES on quality, grades 4-12, and all listed values (0.82, 0.82, 0.75, 0.70, 0.50, prewriting 0.32, models 0.25, grammar -0.32). '5 studies' for sentence combining and 'mostly US' not verified (abstract-only).

claim: Writing about content in science, social studies and mathematics improved learning with an effect size of 0.30 across 56 experiments in grades 1-12, equally across subjects and school levels.
source: Graham, S., Kiuhara, S.A. & MacKay, M. (2020). The effects of writing on learning in science, social studies, and mathematics: a meta-analysis. Review of Educational Research 90(2), 179-226.
effect: 0.30 (95% CI 0.20–0.41 per a secondary summary; not checked in the paper)
population: grades 1-12
recommendation: keep and extend short written production (explain-back, typed missing link) alongside MCQ
risk: low
mark_note: Abstract confirms k=56, grades 1-12, ES=0.30, equally effective across science/social studies/maths and elementary/middle/high. CI 0.20-0.41 not verified (abstract-only).

claim: Across 57 experiments with 336 tests, case-comparison activities produced greater learning than other forms of case study or traditional instruction (d = .50, 95% CI [.44, .56]), with larger effects when learners sought similarities, principles were given after comparison, and testing was immediate.
source: Alfieri, L., Nokes-Malach, T.J. & Schunn, C.D. (2013). Learning through case comparisons: a meta-analytic review. Educational Psychologist 48(2), 87-113.
population: mixed ages, laboratory and classroom
recommendation: comparison items (two evaluation points against data, C4 variant); give the principle after the comparison
risk: immediate-test effects are larger; delayed effects are smaller
mark_note: Abstract confirms 57 experiments, 336 tests, d=.50 95% CI [.44,.56], 15 moderators with 4 significant; similarities, principles after comparison, immediate testing (also perceptual content) associated with greater learning. Abstract-only.

claim: In two sections of an introductory biology course, the section given high-level quizzes and exams all term outperformed the low-level section on both the 20 low-level and 21 high-level final-exam questions.
source: Jensen, J.L., McDaniel, M.A., Woodard, S.M. & Kummer, T.A. (2014). Teaching to the Test...or Testing to Teach: Exams Requiring Higher Order Thinking Skills Encourage Greater Conceptual Understanding. Educational Psychology Review 26(2), 307-329.
population: US undergraduates, introductory biology, two sections
recommendation: shift check mix from definition MCQs towards chain and evaluation checks as mastery rises
risk: test expectancy may explain part of it; one course
mark_note: ERIC abstract: two inquiry-taught intro biology sections, high- vs low-level quizzes/exams all semester; same final with 20 low-level and 21 high-level items; high-level section did better on both. Abstract-only.

claim: Fill-in-the-blank retrieval practice of related premises improved later recall of the premises compared with rereading but did not improve performance on multiple-choice deductive-inference questions.
source: Tran, R., Rohrer, D. & Pashler, H. (2015). Retrieval practice: the lack of transfer to deductive inferences. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 22, 135-140.
population: adult laboratory participants
recommendation: don't expect point-by-point recall checks to build chains of reasoning
risk: low
mark_note: PubMed abstract: four experiments; fill-in-the-blank tests vs rereading of premises; better premise recall; no enhancement on multiple-choice inference questions. Abstract-only.

claim: Retrieval practice did not aid inference when sentences were presented one at a time, but when the sentences of a set were presented simultaneously, fill-in-the-blank testing and free recall aided deductive inference on a test 2 days later more than rereading.
source: Eglington, L.G. & Kang, S.H.K. (2018). Retrieval Practice Benefits Deductive Inference. Educational Psychology Review (online 2016).
population: adult laboratory participants
recommendation: show the whole chain together in chain checks (rec 5)
risk: conflicts with "one point per message"; scope the exception to chain tasks
mark_note: ERIC abstract: 3 experiments, 4 sets of 7-9 sentences, 2-day delay; no benefit with one-at-a-time presentation (from Tran et al.), benefit over rereading with simultaneous presentation (fill-in-blank Exps 1-2, free recall Exp 3). Abstract-only.

claim: Fill-in-the-map concept-map scores placed students close to the maximum possible, whereas construct-a-map-from-scratch scores revealed incomplete knowledge relative to a criterion map, so the two techniques gave different interpretations of students' knowledge structure.
source: Ruiz-Primo, M.A., Schultz, S.E., Li, M. & Shavelson, R.J. (2001). Comparison of the reliability and validity of scores from two concept-mapping techniques. Journal of Research in Science Teaching 38(2), 260-278.
population: school science students (details not in abstract)
recommendation: count selection evidence at reduced weight, and never use it for readiness (rec 6)
risk: low
mark_note: Abstract matches: fill-in-the-map scores near maximum, construct-a-map revealed incomplete knowledge vs criterion map; different interpretations of knowledge structure. Abstract-only.

claim: In an action-research comparison across semesters of a US undergraduate business course (ECO 305, The International Context of Business), structured writing assignments improved performance on lower-order (knowledge and comprehension) assessments but only weakly enhanced performance on higher-order skills assessments.
source: Dynan, L. & Cate, T. (2009). The Impact of Writing Assignments on Student Learning: Should Writing Assignments Be Structured or Unstructured? International Review of Economics Education 8(1), 64-86.
effect: not reported in the extracted text
population: US undergraduates, College of Business course ECO 305, six sections (about 210 students), spring 2005 to fall 2006
recommendation: don't claim that structured practice alone lifts essay marks; pilot with blind levelling (rec 10)
risk: small, confounded by semester
mark_note: Claim rewritten: course is ECO 305 International Context of Business, not principles of economics; design spans 2005-2006. Verifier: Full text: finding matches (structured writing improved lower-order MCQ assessments; structure only weakly enhanced higher-order). But the course is ECO 305 'The International Context of Business' (College of Business, Midwest US), not a principles of economics course; design spans spring 2005-fall 2006, six sections (~210 students): structured in spring 2005/2006, unstructured two sections fall 2006, one no-writing section spring 2005.

claim: Mistral requires users of its products to be at least 13, and minors need parental or legal guardian permission to create an account; the consumer terms for users outside the European Economic Area add 'where required' and limit use to a personal capacity.
source: Mistral AI Help Center, 'Can children use Mistral AI products and services?' (12 Aug 2026); Mistral AI, Terms of Service for consumers outside of the European Union (effective 12 Oct 2026)
population: Mistral consumers worldwide aged 13+
recommendation: Name Le Chat as the only documented consumer route for 16–17-year-olds, with parental permission. Present it as a fallback, not the school route.
risk: credibility, if it is presented as school-approved. Privacy: consumer terms, no school DPA.
mark_note: Claim rewritten: terms are for consumers outside the EEA, not the EU. Verifier: Help page (dated 12 Aug 2026) says 13+ and parental/legal guardian permission for minors creating an account. Consumer terms (effective 12 Oct 2026) add 'where required' and 'solely in your personal capacity'. One error: the terms page is titled 'for consumers outside of the European Economic Area', not 'outside the EU'.

claim: Le Chat custom MCP connectors can only be added by admins, account owners on Free, Pro and Student plans are admins by default, and the supported authentication is none, HTTP bearer/basic in the Authorization header, or OAuth 2.1 with dynamic client registration; Mistral's commercial terms forbid letting minors use the products without legally adequate parent or guardian consent.
source: Mistral AI Docs, 'MCP Connectors' (Le Chat); Mistral AI Commercial Terms of Service s.2.2(c) (effective 25 Sep 2026)
population: Le Chat users and commercial customers
recommendation: An adult tests eduX on Le Chat Free with a bearer header. If it works, list it as a second tested client.
risk: Untested. The docs don't say who administers Team or Enterprise plans.
mark_note: Docs say adding MCP connectors (directory or custom) is administrator-only, and on Free/Pro/Student plans the account owner is the administrator by default. Auth options are No authentication, HTTP Bearer/Basic in the Authorization header, and OAuth 2.1 with DCR. Commercial terms (effective 25 Sep 2026) s.2.2(c) cover children under 13 and minors without 'legally adequate consent from their parent or guardian'. Note: the page now calls the product 'Work' (Vibe Work), with 'Chat (legacy)' alongside, not 'Le Chat'.

claim: Copilot Studio connects agents to existing MCP servers over the Streamable transport only (SSE unsupported after August 2025), with authentication of none, an API key supplied by the agent's user in a header or query parameter, or OAuth 2.0 in Dynamic discovery, Dynamic or Manual modes; Power Platform data policies govern MCP access.
source: Microsoft Learn, 'Connect your agent to an existing Model Context Protocol (MCP) server' (ms.date 6 Nov 2026)
population: Microsoft 365 / Power Platform tenants
recommendation: Use the header API key now and OAuth Manual with the school's Entra app for pilots. Put the steps on the deployment slide.
risk: Untested end to end; third-party vendors report DCR failures with Copilot Studio (secondary sources).
mark_note: Matches the page (ms.date 2026-11-06): Streamable transport only, with SSE unsupported after August 2025. Auth options are None, API key (Header or Query; the agent's user supplies the key), or OAuth 2.0 (Dynamic discovery, Dynamic or Manual). The page says data policies on Power Platform connectors also regulate MCP access.

claim: In K-12 Microsoft 365 Education tenants Copilot Chat is off by default for students aged 13-17 and unavailable under 13, and admins enable it by setting the Education Tenant Identifier to K-12 and the student's ageGroup to NotAdult, with an A1/A3/A5 student licence required; Microsoft's en-GB education page instead says Copilot Chat is available to 'higher education students aged 13 and older'.
source: Microsoft Learn, 'Enable Copilot Chat for learners' (M365 Education); Microsoft, 'Copilot in education' en-GB FAQ
population: students aged 13-17 in Microsoft 365 Education tenants
recommendation: Steps 2–3 of the deployment story. Note the conflicting marketing page in Q&A prep.
risk: Credibility, if a judge reads the en-GB marketing page. Q&A threads report propagation delays (anecdotal).
mark_note: Learn page (updated 2026-09-03): off by default for ages 13-17 in K-12 tenants and blocked under 13. Admins set the Education Tenant Identifier to K-12 and AgeGroup to notAdult, and the page says to confirm an eligible A1/A3/A5 student licence. The en-GB page says Copilot Chat is 'currently available to faculty, staff, and higher education students aged 13 and older'.

claim: The MCP authorization specification requires protected MCP servers to implement OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728) and validate token audience (RFC 8707), forbids access tokens in the URI query string, requires clients to use PKCE S256 and refuse to proceed if code_challenge_methods_supported is absent, makes Client ID Metadata Documents SHOULD and Dynamic Client Registration MAY, and the 2026-07-28 version marks DCR deprecated.
source: Model Context Protocol Specification, 'Authorization', versions 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28
population: n/a (protocol specification)
recommendation: eduX implements only the resource-server duties (PRM, 401 + WWW-Authenticate, audience check, header-only tokens) and relies on an external AS.
risk: Security, if a homemade AS is rushed.
mark_note: Both versions say MCP servers MUST implement RFC 9728 and MUST validate that tokens were issued for them as audience (RFC 8707 s.2). Both say access tokens MUST NOT be in the URI query string, clients MUST use S256, and clients MUST refuse to proceed if code_challenge_methods_supported is absent. CIMD is SHOULD and DCR is MAY. The 2026-07-28 version adds 'Dynamic Client Registration is deprecated and retained for backwards compatibility'.

claim: Copilot Studio bills agent use by users without a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence at 1 Copilot Credit per classic answer, 2 per generative answer, 5 per agent action and 10 for tenant graph grounding, with reasoning models adding 10 credits per 1,000 billed tokens (Microsoft's example: 141 or 461 credits for one message) and prepaid tenants blocked at 125% of capacity unless pay-as-you-go is linked; the US$0.01 per credit pay-as-you-go price comes from Microsoft licensing guidance via a search summary, not the cited page.
source: Microsoft Learn, 'Billing rates and management - Microsoft Copilot Studio' (ms.date 30 Oct 2026); Microsoft Learn, AI Builder 'Licensing and Copilot Credits' (US$0.01 per credit, search snippet)
evidence_strength: official document. The cost per turn is our derived estimate.
effect: our estimate: about 7 credits (about US$0.07) per tutor_turn with a non-reasoning model. About 8,400 credits (about US$84) per student per year at 40 turns per week × 30 weeks (our choice).
population: Copilot Studio tenants
recommendation: Business plan line; deployment step 6 (a non-reasoning model and a monthly cap per agent).
risk: Unconfirmed whether an MCP tool call counts as one agent action. Turn volume is our choice.
mark_note: Claim rewritten: US$0.01/credit not on the cited page (secondary). Verifier: The billing page (ms.date 2026-10-30) confirms 1/2/5/10 credits, with no charge for M365 Copilot-licensed users. It confirms the reasoning-model premium of 10 credits per 1,000 tokens, the 141 and 461 credit examples, and 125% enforcement that blocks agents unless overage goes to pay-as-you-go. The US$0.01/credit figure is not on the cited AI Builder page; a search summary attributes it to Microsoft licensing guidance (microsoft.com/licensing/guidance/Microsoft-Copilot-Studio), but that page was not opened. The per-student cost is the authors' own estimate. Superseded by w3-08m-13 (≈£22.50/student/year).

claim: Microsoft says DCR isn't available for an MCP server protected by Microsoft Entra ID because Entra publishes no RFC 7591 registration endpoint, and the Entra v2.0 OpenID discovery document contains no registration_endpoint, code_challenge_methods_supported or client_id_metadata_document_supported keys; M365 Copilot DCR also requires the authorization server to issue a client secret.
source: Microsoft Learn, 'Configure dynamic client registration' (M365 Copilot plugins, ms.date 10 Nov 2026); Microsoft identity platform v2.0 OpenID configuration document (read 18 Nov 2026)
population: Microsoft Entra-protected MCP servers
recommendation: With Entra, use Copilot Studio **Manual** OAuth (static client). For other clients, put a broker AS in front.
risk: Spec-strict clients may refuse Entra directly. That is a third-party report and unverified for claude.ai and ChatGPT.
mark_note: The DCR page (ms.date 2026-11-10) says DCR isn't available for Entra-protected MCP servers because Entra publishes no RFC 7591 registration endpoint, and that the authorization server must issue a client secret. The live Entra v2.0 discovery document has 25 top-level keys and none of registration_endpoint, code_challenge_methods_supported or client_id_metadata_document_supported.

claim: ChatGPT's MCP OAuth supports Client ID Metadata Documents (preferred), Dynamic Client Registration or a predefined OAuth client, requires PKCE with S256 advertised in code_challenge_methods_supported, and cannot present custom API keys or customer-provided mTLS certificates.
source: OpenAI Developers, Apps SDK 'Authentication' (undated; references MCP 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28)
population: ChatGPT app / MCP server developers
recommendation: Keep `?key=` only for ChatGPT testing. Any OAuth AS must support CIMD or DCR, plus S256 metadata.
risk: none beyond wave 1
mark_note: The page lists CIMD (preferred), DCR and predefined OAuth clients. It says code_challenge_methods_supported must include S256 or the server is unsupported, and that ChatGPT cannot 'present custom API keys or customer-provided mTLS certificates'.

claim: claude.ai custom connectors offer Sign in now, Sign in when needed or No sign in, let the OAuth client be Claude's published identity (marked Recommended), dynamic registration or the user's own client ID, and send fixed credentials such as API keys as request headers on every request, with Authorization unavailable as a header when OAuth is used.
source: Claude.ai Documentation, 'Add a connector that isn't in the directory'; Claude Help Center, 'Get started with custom connectors using remote MCP'
population: claude.ai users
recommendation: Accept the key in a header and update the README so claude.ai users put it in a request header instead of the URL.
risk: Demo connector URLs change if `?key=` is removed. Keep both during the demo.
mark_note: Claim rewritten: published identity is 'Recommended', not the default. Verifier: Sign-in options (Sign in now / when needed / No sign-in) and OAuth client options (published identity, Register automatically via DCR, own client ID) match. Request headers carry fixed credentials on every request, and Authorization can't be set as a header on an OAuth connection. Minor: the docs call the published identity 'Recommended', not the default.

claim: RFC 6750 states that sending bearer tokens as a URI query parameter SHOULD NOT be used unless header or body transport is impossible, because of the high likelihood the URL will be logged, and recommends bearer tokens not be passed in page URLs.
source: Jones, M. & Hardt, D. (2012). RFC 6750: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework: Bearer Token Usage, sections 2.3 and 5.3. IETF.
population: n/a (standard)
recommendation: Move the key to a header (rec 3). In Q&A, cite logging as the reason.
risk: none
mark_note: Section 2.3 says that, because of the 'high likelihood that the URL containing the access token will be logged', it 'SHOULD NOT be used unless it is impossible' to use the header or body. Section 5.3 says 'Bearer tokens SHOULD NOT be passed in page URLs'.

claim: NCSC's 'Securing HTTP-based APIs' guidance (published 3 April 2025) tells organisations not to use weak authentication methods such as basic authentication or API keys, recommends signed JWTs or certificates, and says credentials should be short-lived and automatically rotated or renewed, citing RFC 9700, RFC 8705 and DPoP (RFC 9449).
source: National Cyber Security Centre, 'Securing HTTP-based APIs: 2. API authentication and authorisation' (3 Apr 2025)
population: UK organisations
recommendation: Pitch the keys as a stop-gap. The roadmap is school SSO (Entra) via OAuth.
risk: credibility, if keys are presented as final
mark_note: Page reads 'Published 3 April 2025'. It says 'Don't use weak authentication methods such as basic authentication or API keys', recommends signed JWTs or certificates, and says credentials 'should be automatically rotated or renewed', or made short-lived where storage or replay resistance is weak. It links RFC 9700, RFC 8705 and RFC 9449 (DPoP).

claim: The DfE cyber security standards for schools and colleges (updated 16 September 2026) require unique credentials for each user, require MFA for staff accounts with cloud or remote access and for IT admin accounts but not for students, expect a DPIA for cloud services processing personal data, and do not address keys or tokens in URLs.
source: Department for Education, 'Cyber security standards for schools and colleges', Meeting digital and technology standards in schools and colleges (updated 16 Sep 2026)
population: schools and colleges in England
recommendation: Never claim DfE "compliance" or "non-compliance" for the key. Offer schools a DPIA template and supplier security sheet (deployment step 8).
risk: credibility, from overclaiming compliance
mark_note: Page shows published 23 Mar 2022 and updated 16 Sep 2026, with 7 standards. It requires unique credentials, and MFA for staff accounts with cloud or remote access and for IT admin accounts (none for students). It says to ask the DPO for a DPIA when a cloud service stores or processes personal data, and lock out after no more than 10 attempts. Neither 'token' nor 'query string' appears on the page.

claim: Microsoft message MC1509805 (15 October 2026) says additional content-safety protections switch on automatically from mid-October 2026 for users aged 13-17 identified as teens in Entra ID, including Copilot-integrated apps and agents 'where applicable', without stating that custom or MCP agents are blocked.
source: Microsoft 365 Message Center MC1509805, 'Microsoft Copilot: Additional content safety protections for students under 18' (15 Oct 2026), via third-party mirror
population: users aged 13-17 in Microsoft tenants
recommendation: Mention in the deployment story that Microsoft's teen safeguards sit around eduX automatically.
risk: How far the protections reach custom agents is unspecified.
mark_note: Mirror shows MC1509805 published 15 Oct 2026, with GA beginning mid-October 2026. Protections switch on automatically for ages 13-17 identified by the teen ageGroup in Entra ID, and the scope lists 'Copilot-integrated apps and agents where applicable'. Nothing says custom or MCP agents are blocked. This was checked on a third-party mirror only.

claim: OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teachers is limited to verified US K-12 school staff and is not offered to students, and since 18 August 2026 users estimated or stated to be 13-17 are placed in ChatGPT for Teens; no readable OpenAI page states whether teen accounts can add custom MCP connectors.
source: OpenAI Help Center, 'ChatGPT for Teachers'; OpenAI, 'ChatGPT for Teens' (search snippets only; pages returned 403)
population: US K-12 staff; users aged 13-17
recommendation: Keep ChatGPT as "untested, adult accounts" on the slide. Don't name ChatGPT Edu as a school route.
risk: Snippets may be out of date.
mark_note: Snippet only. Both OpenAI pages returned 403 to curl and WebFetch, and the search budget was used up, so nothing about ChatGPT for Teachers eligibility or the 18 Aug 2026 Teens rollout could be checked independently.

claim: In a cluster RCT in Maine (grade 7 maths), ASSISTments online homework with hints, teacher reports and teacher training benefited low-prior students most; secondary sources give g = 0.18 overall and g = 0.29 for low-prior students; 2,850 students in 43 schools were analysed (46 recruited, 45 randomised).
source: Roschelle, J., Feng, M., Murphy, R. F., & Mason, C. A. (2016). Online mathematics homework increases student achievement. AERA Open 2(4). Effect sizes via Blueprints for Healthy Youth Development and SRI (secondary).
effect: g = 0.18 (SRI report: t(20) = 2.99, p = 0.007); g = 0.29 low-prior; CI not retrieved
population: US grade 7 students, Maine public schools
recommendation: Cite as "online homework with teacher reports" in the pitch. It tests a bundle, so don't attribute the effect to the report alone.
risk: credibility, if presented as a dashboard effect or as A-level evidence
mark_note: Claim rewritten: 45 randomised, not 46; effect sizes secondary only. Verifier: Abstract (OpenAlex) confirms 2,850 grade 7 students, 43 schools, Maine; intervention = hints/feedback + teacher reports + training; low-prior benefited most. g=0.18 / 0.29 and 6.5% school attrition confirmed only via Blueprints (secondary). '46 randomised' is wrong: Blueprints says 46 recruited, 1 withdrew before assignment so 45 randomised, then 1 treatment school and its matched pair dropped -> 43. TerraNova named by Evidence for ESSA (secondary). Full text not accessible (SAGE 403).

claim: A follow-up analysis of the Maine ASSISTments trial reported g = 0.22 in a three-level model and no significant indirect effect through teachers' targeted homework review practices.
source: Murphy, R., Roschelle, J., Feng, M., & Mason, C. A. (2020). Investigating efficacy, moderators and mediators for an online mathematics homework intervention. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness 13(2), 235-270 (via Blueprints, secondary).
effect: g = 0.22; mediation not significant (no figure retrieved)
population: US grade 7 students, Maine
recommendation: Don't claim that the teacher-report channel drives gains. Design the view to make an in-class action easy (the starter MCQ), and measure its use in pilots.
risk: credibility
mark_note: Blueprints (secondary) confirms g=.22 three-level model and no significant indirect effect via targeted homework review. Abstract confirms 43 schools, 87 teachers, 2,769 students and 'mediating role of this practice was unclear'. Secondary only.

claim: A North Carolina replication of ASSISTments (63 schools, 9,073 grade 7 students enrolled, about 6,000 analysed) found an effect size of about +0.10 on the grade 8 state maths test one year after the programme, with grade 7 outcomes lost to COVID-19; a second grade 8 readiness test showed no significant effect.
source: WestEd/IES ASSISTments replication study, as reported by Evidence for ESSA and Evidence-Based Programs (secondary).
population: US grade 7-8 students, North Carolina
recommendation: Quote the smaller replication alongside the original when asked "does it replicate?".
risk: low
mark_note: Claim rewritten: 9,073 is enrolment; about 6,000 analysed; WWC reports a non-significant second outcome (secondary only). Verifier: Secondary only. Evidence-Based Programs: 63 schools, 9,073 seventh graders, grade 7 outcomes lost to COVID, effect at end of grade 8. Evidence for ESSA: ES +0.10 on NC grade 8 EOG maths. Note the analytic sample per Evidence for ESSA was ~6,000 (2,961 T / 3,030 C), so 9,073 is enrolment, not students analysed. WWC record reports non-significant result on a second grade 8 readiness test.

claim: A systematic review of 38 studies found no evidence that learning analytics dashboards improve academic achievement (mostly negligible or small effects), while several studies reported medium to large effects on participation.
source: Kaliisa, R., Misiejuk, K., López-Pernas, S., Khalil, M., & Saqr, M. (2024). Have learning analytics dashboards lived up to the hype? A systematic review of impact on students' achievement, motivation, participation and attitude. LAK '24, ACM.
effect: not reported (systematic review, no pooled estimate; narrative: negligible or small for achievement)
population: Students in mixed, mostly higher-education/online settings
recommendation: Don't promise attainment gains from the view. Promise an action (a reteach starter), and measure re-check accuracy in pilots.
risk: credibility if overclaimed
mark_note: arXiv abstract matches: 38 studies, no evidence LADs improved achievement (mostly negligible/small effects), several medium-to-large effects on participation. Abstract-only (full text PDF not extractable here); population description 'mostly higher-education/online' not checked.

claim: A systematic review of teacher-facing learning analytics dashboards included 50 of 1,968 retrieved articles and found dashboards mostly at prototype or pilot stage, with evaluation dominated by self-reports and user reactions.
source: Kaliisa, R., Jivet, I., & Prinsloo, P. (2023). A checklist to guide the planning, designing, implementation, and evaluation of learning analytics dashboards. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education 20.
effect: not reported (systematic review, no pooled estimate)
population: Higher-education teachers
recommendation: Plan a pilot outcome beyond satisfaction (rec 8).
risk: low
mark_note: Abstract matches exactly: 1,968 retrieved, 50 included, teacher-facing dashboards, deployed at prototype and pilot stages, evaluation dominated by self-reports and users' reactions. Abstract-only (Springer redirects blocked).

claim: In an experiment with 286 students in 18 US middle-school classes (8 teachers), teachers' real-time analytics glasses improved learning with an intelligent tutor versus business as usual and monitoring without analytics, and narrowed gaps by prior ability; press coverage reports more than half the gain came from glasses with analytics off.
source: Holstein, K., McLaren, B. M., & Aleven, V. (2018). Student learning benefits of a mixed-reality teacher awareness tool in AI-enhanced classrooms. AIED 2018, LNCS 10947, 154-168; Hechinger Report coverage (journalism) for the 'more than half' figure.
population: US middle-school maths students (grades 7-8)
recommendation: Treat "being watched" as an active ingredient that cuts both ways. eduX's view is asynchronous and class-level, so it shouldn't claim this effect.
risk: surveillance framing; credibility
mark_note: Abstract summary (Stanford SCALE) confirms 3-condition experiment, 286 middle-school students, 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, analytics beat business-as-usual and monitoring without analytics, may narrow gaps by prior ability. Hechinger 'psychological impact of student surveillance' article does say more than half the learning gains came from teachers wearing the functionally limited glasses (the cited 'these glasses give teachers superpowers' article does not). Full paper not accessible; grades 7-8 not verified.

claim: In Dutch primary classrooms, teachers consulted an adaptive-learning dashboard on average 8.3 times per lesson with large variation, and their follow-up actions were mainly individual feedback and extra instruction.
source: Molenaar, I., & Knoop-van Campen, C. (2017). Teacher dashboards in practice: usage and impact. EC-TEL 2017, LNCS 10474; Molenaar & Knoop-van Campen (2019), How teachers make dashboard information actionable, IEEE TLT 12(3), 347-355 (via secondary summaries).
population: Dutch primary teachers and pupils
recommendation: Put the action next to the signal: a starter MCQ beside each flagged misconception.
risk: low
mark_note: Could not open either paper (Springer/IEEE/Radboud repository blocked; publisher elides abstract in OpenAlex/S2). The 8.3 consultations per lesson and the follow-up actions are unverified here; claim itself flags secondary summaries.

claim: Across 35 K-12 classrooms, dashboard-prompted teacher feedback was balanced between task and process feedback, whereas human-prompted feedback (teacher-initiated or in response to student questions) leaned towards task feedback, most strongly for low-ability students.
source: Knoop-van Campen, C. A. N., Wise, A., & Molenaar, I. (2023). The equalizing effect of teacher dashboards on feedback in K-12 classrooms. Interactive Learning Environments 31(6), 3447-3463.
population: K-12 classrooms (Dutch per scout; not stated in abstract)
recommendation: A class-level misconception list directs reteaching to the idea, not to "the usual students". Use this in the Q&A on fairness.
risk: low

claim: In an RCT with about 1,000 Turkish high-school students in about 50 grade 9-11 classes randomised by class over four 90-minute sessions, unrestricted GPT-4 (GPT Base) raised practice scores by 48% but reduced unassisted exam scores by 17% (-0.054, SE 0.022), while a guarded GPT Tutor raised practice scores by 127% with no significant exam effect (-0.004, SE 0.013).
source: Bastani, H., Bastani, O., Sungu, A., Ge, H., Kabakci, O. & Mariman, R. (2025). Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics. PNAS 122(26), e2422633122.

population: ~1,000 students, grades 9-11, one high school in Turkey, Fall 2023
