claim: Using the large-sample standard error of Cohen's kappa, a 95% CI at kappa = .7 and prevalence .5 has half-width about .22 at n = 40, .16 at n = 80 and .10 at n = 200; a half-width of .15 needs about 88 decisions (107 at prevalence .3) and .10 needs about 196 (240).
source: Our calculation using Cohen's large-sample approximation to the SE of kappa, SE ≈ sqrt[po(1−po)/(n(1−pe)^2)] (Cohen J (1960). A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales. Educational and Psychological Measurement 20(1):37–46)
population: hypothetical two-rater binary labels
recommendation: Pool binary decisions within each skill and replace 02's "±.22 on 40 items" line with per-skill pooled figures.
risk: credibility. The CI assumes independent decisions. Clustering within a message widens it (our simulation: ±.16 → ±.18 for the Ask pool), so use the cluster bootstrap.
mark_note: Recomputed (Cohen large-sample SE, equal marginals, kappa .7): half-widths n=40 .221, n=80 .156, n=200 .099; ±.15 needs 88 (π .5)/107 (π .3); ±.10 needs 196/240. All reproduce exactly. Cohen 1960 EPM 20(1):37-46 confirmed via Crossref.

claim: Applying the Donner–Eliasziw goodness-of-fit sample-size formula (equal marginals, power .80, two-sided alpha .05), distinguishing kappa .8 from .4 needs about 42 subjects at prevalence .5, .7 from .4 about 74, and .8 from .6 about 126.
source: Donner A, Eliasziw M (1992). A goodness-of-fit approach to inference procedures for the kappa statistic: confidence interval construction, significance-testing and sample size estimation. Statistics in Medicine 11(11):1511–1519 (formula applied in our calculation)
population: hypothetical two-rater binary labels
recommendation: At n = 40, frame the test as "better than fair (κ > .4)", not "κ is precisely X".
risk: credibility. The formula was reconstructed and not checked against a printed table. An earlier run of ours had a denominator bug (P₁ instead of P₀), which halved n. It was caught by simulation.
mark_note: Recomputed with D-E goodness-of-fit formula (n = (z.975+z.80)^2 / Σ(P_i(κ1)-P_i(κ0))^2/P_i(κ0), 3 cells, equal marginals): .4 vs .8 π .5 → 41.2→42; π .3 → 47.6→48; .4 vs .7 → 73.3→74; .6 vs .8 → 125.6→126; one-sided .4 vs .8 → 32.5→33. All reproduce. Paper metadata (Stat Med 11(11):1511-1519, 1992) confirmed via Crossref; full text not read.

source: Sim J, Wright CC (2005). The kappa statistic in reliability studies: use, interpretation, and sample size requirements. Physical Therapy 85(3):257–268; Bujang MA, Baharum N (2017). Guidelines of the minimum sample size requirements for Kappa agreement test. Epidemiology, Biostatistics and Public Health 14(2)
population: clinical reliability studies (not education, not 16–18)
recommendation: Cite Sim & Wright as the standard reference for the kappa sample-size approach, and show our own computed table.

claim: Gwet (2008) proposes the AC1 coefficient as a more stable alternative to kappa and pi under high agreement (the kappa paradoxes), with variance estimators that do not assume rater independence; in a 40-item example with 90% raw agreement and 87.5% positive prevalence (35 positives per rater, 33 both positive), kappa is about .54 while AC1 is about .87.
source: Gwet KL (2008). Computing inter-rater reliability and its variance in the presence of high agreement. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology 61(1):29–48 (illustration: our calculation)
evidence_strength: theory (plus a Monte Carlo study in the paper)
effect: κ ≈ .54 vs AC1 ≈ .87 at .875 prevalence (verifier's recomputation); κ .28 / AC1 .88 needs marginal prevalence .925
population: general
recommendation: Write the messages so each label is near 50% prevalence, and report AC1 and % agreement next to κ.
risk: credibility. AC1 alone can flatter. Always show κ too.
mark_note: Claim corrected. ~ illustration corrected: at .875 prevalence the table gives κ ≈ .54, AC1 ≈ .87, not κ .28 / AC1 .88 (those figures need marginal prevalence .925; 87.5% was the both-positive cell share). Gwet 2008 checked at abstract level. Verifier: Gwet 2008 (BJMSP 61(1):29-48) abstract confirms AC1 as more stable alternative to pi/kappa (paradoxes) and variance estimators not depending on rater independence (abstract only). Illustration does NOT reproduce as stated: with 40 items, po .90 and 87.5% positive prevalence (35/40 per rater, 33 both-pos), kappa = .54 and AC1 = .87. kappa .28 / AC1 .88 corresponds to 35 both-positive, 2+2 disagreements, 1 both-negative, i.e. marginal prevalence .925 (87.5% is the both-positive cell share, not prevalence).

claim: Hayes and Krippendorff (2007) argue Krippendorff's alpha satisfies the criteria for a standard reliability measure for coding data; the customary thresholds (alpha ≥ .800, with .667 as the lowest limit for tentative conclusions) are attributed to Krippendorff (2004, p. 241) only via secondary sources.
source: Hayes AF, Krippendorff K (2007). Answering the call for a standard reliability measure for coding data. Communication Methods and Measures 1(1):77–89; Krippendorff K (2004). Content Analysis: An Introduction to Its Methodology, 2nd ed., p. 241 (thresholds via secondary source)

claim: In our simulation, a pass rule of kappa ≥ .60 with cluster-bootstrap 95% lower bound ≥ .40 on 72 binary decisions from 18 messages (prevalence .5) passes a rater whose true kappa is .6 in 38–50% of replicates, .7 in 80–89% and .8 in 98–99%; with 40 independent items and a Wald bound the figures are 40%, 74% and 95%.
source: Our simulation (2,000 replicates per cell), eduX overnight research wave 3, w3-02e Appendix C
population: hypothetical
recommendation: State on Thursday that a pass is weak evidence of κ ≥ .6. Use the human ceiling as the second criterion.
risk: credibility, if the pass is reported as proof.
mark_note: Re-simulated (2,000 reps, 1,000 cluster-bootstrap resamples). 72/18 design, no within-message correlation: pass .47-.48 (κ .6), .86-.88 (κ .7), .99 (κ .8), matching the upper ends of the claimed ranges; adding within-message error correlation lowers pass rates (rater-vs-gold, ICC .2: .39/.72/.94), so the lower ends depend on the unspecified clustering model. 40 independent items + Wald bound: .40/.71/.94 (two-rater multinomial) or .44/.75/.96 (rater vs fixed 20/20 key), vs claimed .40/.74/.95 — reproduces within model/MC variation. Used /usr/bin/python3 (venv lacks numpy). Scripts: /tmp/claude-1000/c6.py, c6b.py, c6c.py.

claim: A meta-analysis of 34 studies (119 effect sizes) found test accommodations raised scores more for students with disabilities (mean ES 0.30, k = 62) than for typically developing peers (0.17, k = 57), with timing/scheduling accommodations at 0.47 (k = 17) for students with disabilities; a separate meta-analysis of extra time for adolescents with learning disabilities concluded it raised more questions than answers.

evidence_strength: meta-analysis (one unpublished dissertation; one with inconclusive results)
effect: ES 0.30 vs 0.17; timing 0.47 (CIs not in abstract)
population: US K-12 and postsecondary students with and without disabilities, mostly; not UK
outcome: learning (test scores under accommodation, not learning gains)
recommendation: Extra time helps students with disabilities somewhat more, but everyone gains a little. "No time pressure" is a universal-design default, not a SEND feature. Keep eduX untimed.
risk: mixed evidence. Don't claim eduX "accommodates" SEND, only that it imposes no timing.
mark_note: ~ Vanchu-Orosco figures match via abstract snippets (full text 403); Gregg & Nelson subtitle confirmed only via reference lists. Verifier: Vanchu-Orosco figures (34 studies, 119 ES, 0.30 k=62, 0.17 k=57, timing 0.47 k=17) match abstract via search snippets; DU full text returned 403. Gregg & Nelson subtitle 'More questions than answers' confirmed only via reference lists; abstract not read.

claim: A meta-analysis of 23 group-design studies found text-to-speech/read-aloud tools improved reading comprehension for students with reading disabilities, d = 0.35, 95% CI [0.14, 0.56], with grade level and reader type not significant moderators and within-subject studies averaging 0.15 versus 0.61 for between-subject designs.

claim: A meta-analysis of 80 years of research found that reducing multiple-choice items from four or five options to three had little or no average effect on item difficulty, discrimination or score reliability, concluding three options are optimal in most settings.
source: Rodriguez, M. C. (2005), Three options are optimal for multiple-choice items: a meta-analysis of 80 years of research, Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice 24(2), 3-13
effect: "little to no" change (numbers not in abstract)
population: mostly school-age test takers, US; not 16–18 UK-specific
recommendation: `mcq.max_options = 3` (our choice). Each check is a third shorter to read, and needs fewer invented options (rec 4).
risk: low. A three-option item has a higher guess rate (33%), which BKT's guess parameter must reflect: `settings.toml` sets `mcq_check` guess = 0.25 ("about 1 in 4"), so raise it to about 0.33 with the change.
mark_note: Claim corrected. ~ abstract confirms 80 years and the 3-option conclusion but gives no study count; "43 studies, mostly school-based" removed (secondary; another summary says 27). Full text paywalled. Verifier: Abstract (via OpenAlex) confirms 80 years and 3-option endorsement without psychometric harm, but gives no study count. '43 studies' and 'mostly school-aged' come from Raymond et al. 2019 (secondary); another summary says 27 articles. Full text paywalled (403).

claim: In eduX's example pack, every one of the 9 parts with misconceptions shows a correct MCQ option that differs in form from its own distractors: 7 use the node description, a topic label such as 'Calculating PED from percentage changes in quantity demanded and price.', because those parts have no mark points, and 2 use mark-scheme wording ('States that…', 'Notes that…'); the correct option is longer than every distractor of its part in 7 of 9 parts (all but ped_formula and pes_formula; correct 10-18 words, distractors 6-15), whereas Haladyna, Downing & Rodriguez's taxonomy of 31 item-writing guidelines advises options that are homogeneous in form and similar in length.
source: Our audit of coursepacks/example-mini (mark_points.csv, misconceptions.csv) and edux/plan.py, 18 Nov 2026; Haladyna, T. M., Downing, S. M. & Rodriguez, M. C. (2002), A review of multiple-choice item-writing guidelines for classroom assessment, Applied Measurement in Education 15(3), 309-333
population: eduX example pack (synthetic)
recommendation: (a) Use the `exemplar` as the correct option's text. (b) Never use the node `description` as an option: warn at ingest, and skip the MCQ check for parts with no mark point. (c) Warn on a length mismatch within a part, and on absolute words ("always") in distractors (rec 1). Per part (correct vs own distractors, in words): ped_definition 12 vs 8/10; ped_formula 10 vs 10/9/15; ped_values 17 vs 8; pes_definition 14 vs 10; pes_formula 10 vs 6/15; yed_definition 12 vs 6; tax_supply_shift 17 vs 7; tax_incidence_split 18 vs 13; externality_tax_eval 11 vs 7.
risk: credibility. A judge trying the demo may notice that the right answer is always the topic-label or "States that…" option. It also inflates BKT mastery. The pack is a tiny synthetic sample, and a real pack with mark points on every part would show only the "States that…" form.
mark_note: Claim corrected. ~ correct option is longest in 7 of 9 parts, not 6 (verifier re-audit, by words and by characters). Verifier: Re-audited coursepacks/example-mini with plan.py logic (_points fallback at plan.py:376; distractors = wrong_idea, max_options 4): 9 parts, 7 description fallback, 2 mark-point, correct 10-18 words, distractors 6-15, all confirmed. But correct option is longer than every distractor in 7 of 9 parts (not 6): only ped_formula and pes_formula are not, by words and by characters. Haladyna et al. 31-guideline count confirmed.

claim: A meta-analysis of accommodations for English language learners on large-scale maths and science tests found none of seven accommodations threatened validity and only English dictionaries or glossaries had a statistically significant (small) effect on ELLs' performance.

risk: the abstract describes simplified English only as not significant. Don't quote a number.
mark_note: ~ abstract only (OpenAlex). Verifier: Abstract only (OpenAlex): seven accommodations, none threatened validity, only English dictionaries/glossaries significant with small effect. Not retracted.

claim: A 20-week academic-vocabulary RCT in 14 US urban middle schools (N = 2,082 sixth-graders, 1,469 from non-English-speaking homes) improved vocabulary, morphological awareness and comprehension of texts with taught words, with larger effects for students whose home language was not English and those with weaker initial vocabulary; a systematic review of EAL interventions found explicit vocabulary instruction gave gains, larger for the lowest pre-test scorers, and a lack of UK studies for ages 14-18.
source: Lesaux, N. K., Kieffer, M. J., Kelley, J. G. & Harris, J. R. (2014), Effects of academic vocabulary instruction for linguistically diverse adolescents, American Educational Research Journal 51(6), 1159-1194; Oxley, E. & de Cat, C. (2019), A systematic review of language and literacy interventions in children and adolescents with English as an additional language (EAL), The Language Learning Journal
effect: not reported in abstracts (direction and moderators only)

recommendation: `teach_point` should name and define the course term in plain words the first time (fits rule 9). The glossary (rec 9) gives each term a home.
risk: this is an extrapolation from 11-year-olds to sixth-formers. Say so.
mark_note: ~ Lesaux abstract confirmed; Oxley & de Cat review points only via search summary. Verifier: Lesaux abstract confirms 20 weeks, 14 schools, N = 2,082, n = 1,469, outcomes and larger effects for non-English home language and weaker vocabulary. Oxley & de Cat points (explicit vocabulary gains, larger for lowest pre-test, lack of UK studies for 14-18) confirmed only via search summary; PDF text not extractable.

claim: In two experiments with children with dyslexia (n = 170; n = 102 plus 45 controls) the Dyslexie font did not improve reading speed or accuracy versus Arial, whereas extra-large letter spacing improved text reading in Italian and French dyslexic children and short lines on a small e-reader improved speed or comprehension for subsets of 103 US high-school students with dyslexia.
source: Kuster, S. M. et al. (2018), Dyslexie font does not benefit reading in children with or without dyslexia, Annals of Dyslexia 68, 25-42; Zorzi, M. et al. (2012), Extra-large letter spacing improves reading in dyslexia, PNAS 109(28), 11455-11459; Schneps, M. H. et al. (2013), E-readers are more effective than paper for some with dyslexia, PLoS ONE 8(9), e75634
effect: null (font). Positive for subsets (spacing, short lines; numbers not in abstracts).

recommendation: Make no font claims. eduX's equivalents of "short lines" are short paragraphs and one point per message, already built. Students can set spacing and fonts in their own device or browser.
risk: overclaiming dyslexia support. eduX doesn't control rendering.
mark_note: ~ Schneps confirmed in full text (subgroup gains only, no main effect); Kuster and Zorzi at abstract level only. Verifier: Schneps full text confirms 103 high-schoolers with dyslexia, subgroup gains only (no main effect). Kuster (170; 102 + 45, vs Arial, no benefit) and Zorzi (Italian and French children, spacing improved text reading) checked only at abstract level.

claim: A meta-analysis of 56 investigations (88 comparisons) found segmenting instructional material had small-to-medium positive effects on retention and transfer.
source: Rey, G. D., Beege, M., Nebel, S., Wirzberger, M., Schmitt, T. H. & Schneider, S. (2019), A meta-analysis of the segmenting effect, Educational Psychology Review 31, 389-419

recommendation: (Weak support only: numbers come from a search snippet, and no recommendation depends on the moderator.) Consistent with one point per message and the 80-word teach cap as a design for all. Don't sell it as a SEND or ADHD intervention. Let students shorten further (rec 2).
risk: the abstract could not be fully read; the reported prior-knowledge moderator (segmenting may help higher-prior learners more) is unconfirmed, so don't present segmenting as a support for weaker learners.

Verifier: 56 investigations, 88 pairwise comparisons, small-to-medium retention and transfer effects confirmed via abstract snippets; higher-prior-knowledge moderator result not confirmed (abstract not fully readable, paywalled).

claim: By a heuristic Flesch-Kincaid count, eduX's example-pack note summaries are at grade 8.4 pooled (reading ease about 60, about 14 words per sentence), within WCAG 2.2's lower-secondary level (7-9 years of schooling), while the chatbot-facing move texts pool at about grade 10.4 with 25.2 words per sentence and 5 of 11 move files average over 25 words per sentence (answer_brief exactly 25.0).

Note-summary figures match. Verifier: Reran a heuristic FK: 9 note summaries give FKGL 8.4, FRE 59.8, 14.1 wps (matches). For the 11 move .md files I got pooled FKGL 10.4 and 25.2 wps with 5 files over 25 wps (answer_brief exactly 25.0), versus claimed 8.8/23.6/4 - depends on markdown preprocessing. claim: A meta-analysis of 34 samples (26 reports, 1997-2010) found intelligent tutoring systems had at most a small effect on K-12 maths learning (average g = 0.01 to 0.09) and were less effective for low achievers than for the general population.
source: Steenbergen-Hu, S. & Cooper, H. (2013), A meta-analysis of the effectiveness of intelligent tutoring systems on K-12 students' mathematical learning, Journal of Educational Psychology 105(4), 970-987

population: US-dominated K-12 maths; not 16–18 UK
recommendation: Don't claim eduX narrows gaps. In the pitch, say that the evidence is mixed and that schools can check uptake and outcomes by their own groups (rec 11).
risk: credibility, if equity is overclaimed. Fairness risk: students with low prior attainment may benefit less.
mark_note: ~ abstract only. Verifier: Abstract only: 26 reports, 34 samples, 1997-2010, g = 0.01 to 0.09 ('no negative and perhaps a small positive effect'), less effective for low achievers than general population. Not retracted.

claim: In a randomised trial in 43 Maine schools with 2,850 seventh-graders, ASSISTments online maths homework raised end-of-year standardised maths scores (reported g = 0.18), with students of low prior maths achievement benefiting most.

risk: over-broad reading of "education functions".
